content: Prenatal and perinatal psychology is an interdisciplinary field that examines the foundational aspects of health in the body, mind, emotions, and long-term behavioral patterns. It investigates the psychological and psychophysiological effects of the earliest experiences of an individual, both before birth (prenatal) and during or immediately after childbirth (perinatal). These early experiences are considered to have significant implications for an individual’s health, learning capacity, and interpersonal relationships. This field has developed a range of therapeutic and preventive interventions aimed at addressing issues in the unborn, during childbirth, and in newborns, infants, and adults who have been negatively impacted by early prenatal and perinatal dysfunction or trauma. Some of these methods, such as homebirth practices in Western societies or the use of LSD psychotherapy to resolve birth trauma in earlier times, have been met with considerable controversy. In neurobiology, it is understood that while experiences can alter the mature brain, experiences during critical periods of early childhood play a pivotal role in organizing brain systems. In psychoneuroendocrinology, evidence suggests the existence of an umbilical affect exchange, which influences both immediate and long-term psychological behaviors. In bioengineering, the importance of the fetomaternal system for development and growth is increasingly recognized. Clinical maternal-fetal medicine explores the unique symbiotic relationship between a mother and her fetus, examining how maternal stress and hormonal mechanisms, particularly the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, may contribute to the development of later psychopathology in the child. Despite the theoretical and psychotherapeutic diversity in approaches to this topic, a common theme is the critical role of prenatal and perinatal experiences in shaping personality and future psychological development. However, this assertion is not widely supported in mainstream psychology, partly due to skepticism about the ability of newborns to form memories, the impact of such memories on personality, and the possibility of recovering these memories from the unconscious mind. Many psychologists question the validity and even the existence of repressed memories, as only a minority have direct experience with therapeutic modalities that explore these phenomena. Nevertheless, it is important to note that experience and memory are not synonymous. While a fetal or infant brain may not recall experiences, those moments were still lived, potentially eliciting neurological, psychological, or physiological responses that could influence the ongoing development of the mind and brain structures. The significance of birth experiences has been acknowledged since the early days of modern psychology. Sigmund Freud briefly considered the idea before rejecting it in favor of the Oedipus complex. However, one of his disciples, Otto Rank, became convinced of the importance of birth trauma in causing anxiety neuroses. Rank developed a psychoanalytic process centered on birth experiences and authored the seminal work The Trauma of Birth. Freud’s initial agreement and subsequent rejection of Rank’s ideas caused a rift between them, relegating the study of birth trauma to the fringes of psychology. In 1949, Nandor Fodor, a patient of Rank and teacher of Francis Mott, revisited the subject, emphasizing the significance of both birth and prenatal trauma. During the 1950s, Donald Winnicott shifted the focus toward non-traumatic aspects of early experiences, while Maarten Lietaert Peerbolte explored transpersonal dimensions, including the relevance of very early gestation and even the event of conception. These ideas were later elaborated upon by figures such as Frank Lake, Michael Irving, R.D. Laing, Graham Farrant, and Stanislav Grof. The broader societal expression of perinatal feelings, such as the suffering fetus or toxic placenta, became part of the narrative in psychohistory, as developed by Lloyd deMause. Prenatal and perinatal psychology also became central to Primal Therapy and Primal Integration. Professor Stephen Maret explored these influences in his book The Prenatal Person. Research into the enduring effects of prenatal and perinatal experiences in adult life was further advanced by Frank Lake, Athanasios Kafkalides, and Stanislav Grof, who utilized material from psychedelic psychotherapy sessions involving LSD and other hallucinogenic drugs. Grof subsequently developed an extensive theoretical framework for analyzing these experiences, based on his concept of the four Basic Perinatal Matrices. Both Lake and Grof independently developed breathing techniques as alternatives to psychedelic drugs, which faced significant legal challenges from the mid-1960s onward. A related technique, Rebirthing Breathwork, was developed by Leonard Orr, and Core Process Psychotherapy trainees relive presumed birth trauma as part of their training. Public awareness of the importance of prenatal experiences was heightened by the 1981 book The Secret Life of the Unborn Child by Thomas R. Verny, who founded the Association for Pre& Perinatal Psychology and Health (APPPAH). David Chamberlain, president of APPPAH from 1991 to 1999, published the book Babies Remember Birth (1988), which outlined experimental research supporting the existence of prenatal memories. Further evidence was presented by Ludwig Janus in The Enduring Effects of Prenatal Experience (1997). One of the first books to effectively convey the importance of trauma-free childbirth to the general public was Birth Without Violence (1975) by French obstetrician Dr. Frederick Leboyer. This book popularized the practice of placing newborns in a tub of warm water, known as the Leboyer bath, to simulate the familiar prenatal environment of warm amniotic fluid. Building on Leboyer’s work, another French obstetrician, Michel Odent, pioneered low-intervention labor and developed the use of warm-water pools for water births. In 2004, Dr. Wendy Anne McCarty, co-founder of the Prenatal and Perinatal Psychology Program at Santa Barbara Graduate Institute, reviewed 30 years of clinical research in the field and current mainstream early development models. In her book Welcoming Consciousness, she introduced the Integrated Model of early development, which reflects the clinical findings of prenatal and perinatal psychology. The transcendental and human aspects of awareness documented from the beginning of life became central to this holonomic, holographic model.
